summary: This note covers Harper Lee's novel To Kill a Mockingbird (1960), set in the fictional town of Maycomb, Alabama, during the Great Depression, and follows Scout, Jem, Dill and their reclusive neighbor Boo Radley. It describes the novel's mixed early reviews, its enormous sales and educational use, and the 1962 film adaptation with Gregory Peck. It also covers the annual Monroeville stage play since 1990 and Lee's life, including her friendship with Truman Capote, who inspired the character of Dill.
one_line: Overview of Harper Lee's 1960 novel To Kill a Mockingbird, its plot, reception, film and stage adaptations, and the author's life.
key_facts: To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel by Harper Lee published in 1960 that was immediately successful, winning the Pulitzer Prize.
The story takes place during three years (1933–35) of the Great Depression in the fictional 'tired old town' of Maycomb, Alabama.
The novel focuses on six-year-old Jean Louise Finch (Scout), her older brother Jem, and their widowed father Atticus, a middle-aged lawyer.
The 1962 film of To Kill a Mockingbird starred Gregory Peck as Atticus Finch and won three Oscars, including Best Actor for Gregory Peck.
The film quickly grossed more than $20 million from a $2-million budget, according to the note.
Horton Foote won the Oscar for Best Writing, Screenplay Based on Material from Another Medium for the 1962 film.
Mary Badham, who played Scout, was nominated for Best Actress in a Supporting Role at the Oscars.
Since 1990, a play by Christopher Sergel based on the novel has been performed annually in Monroeville, Alabama, running every May on the county courthouse grounds with townspeople as the cast.
The novel has sold more than 30 million copies and been translated into more than 40 languages.
A 1991 survey by the Book of the Month Club and the Library of Congress Center for the Book found the novel rated behind only the Bible in books 'most often cited as making a difference'.
Lee modeled the character of Dill on her childhood friend Truman Capote, known then as Truman Persons.
Granville Hicks labeled the book 'melodramatic and contrived' in a review that also criticized its portrayal of poor white Southerners.
Atticus tells Jem that courage is 'when you're licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what'.
Born in 1926, Harper Lee attended Huntingdon College in Montgomery (1944–45) and studied law at the University of Alabama (1945–49).
In 1950 Lee moved to New York City, where she worked as a reservation clerk for British Overseas Airways Corporation.
